blocks.x: An empty storefront costs more than lost rent. It can drag down the whole strip, discourage neighbouring tenants and make the space harder to lease the longer it sits. A focused vacant storefront renovation can help turn a showing into a signed lease.
Sometimes the issue isn't the location. It's that prospective tenants can't picture their business in a tired, dated or oddly configured space.
Why retail spaces sit empty
**Dated look:** old flooring, dropped ceilings, poor lighting and faded storefronts.
**Hard-to-use layout:** odd shapes, too much back-of-house or awkward columns.
**Missing basics:** no accessible washroom, tired HVAC, limited electrical capacity.
**Unknown costs:** tenants worry about what it will cost to make the space work.
The landlord's vacant storefront renovation playbook
1. Fix the storefront first

The façade is your best advertisement. Clean or [repair masonry](/services/masonry-stucco), refresh paint, improve signage areas, upgrade the entry door and add exterior lighting. A bright, clean storefront gets noticed.

In its downtown program area, the [Storefront Success grant](/blog/how-to-finance-a-commercial-renovation-without-breaking-the-bank) covers storefront, façade, lighting, signage, entrance and accessibility work, and its priorities include businesses occupying previously vacant storefronts. Businesses apply through CentreVenture. The Province's release doesn't mention landlords, so ask CentreVenture whether and how a landlord fits in.
The remaining deadlines are December 31, 2026 and March 31, 2027, and funding may run out sooner. Bridgeland Builders has no role in the program.
2. Deliver a "vanilla box"
Many small retailers want a clean, neutral space they can finish themselves. A typical vanilla box includes:
Smooth, painted walls and a finished ceiling
Basic lighting throughout
A working, accessible washroom
HVAC in good repair
Electrical panel and outlets ready for tenant use
Flooring ready for finishes (or a durable finished floor)
It can shorten the tenant's fit-out and makes your space easy to compare against others.
3. Bring the space up to code

Accessibility, fire separations, exits and washroom requirements can surprise new tenants. Addressing them in advance removes one reason deals fall apart. What applies depends on the building and the next tenant's use, so ask a registered architect or engineer before you spend.
4. Consider splitting or combining units

If demand is for smaller shops, splitting a large unit can lease faster. If a neighbour wants to expand, combining units may be the answer. Either way, check the permits first: the City calls for an occupancy permit when a unit's size changes, and new walls between tenants generally need a registered architect or engineer.
5. Offer a clear tenant improvement package

Let tenants know what you'll provide (a vanilla box, a dollar allowance, or a turnkey build-out) so they can make decisions fast. Our guide to [tenant improvement allowances](/blog/tenant-improvement-allowance-winnipeg) covers who pays for what.
Permits for retail renovation in Winnipeg

Most retail renovations need a City of Winnipeg building permit. Cosmetic work such as flooring and painting generally doesn't, though any electrical, plumbing or ventilation work needs a trade permit, and any change to a sign needs its own permit.

A change of use (for example, retail to restaurant or clinic) starts with a building permit application, even with little or no construction, then needs an occupancy permit before the space is used. It may also require additional upgrades.
Our guide to [occupancy permits and change of use](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg) explains the steps. Plan permit time into your leasing timeline.

If the whole building is empty, ask the City about its [Renovation Fee Waiver and Vacant Building Exemption programs](https://www.winnipeg.ca/news/2026-06-15-city-launching-new-programs-support-vacant-building-redevelopment), open since July 1, 2026. They offer credits or exemptions on vacant building fees for owners who are redeveloping. The City's pages don't say whether one empty unit in an occupied building qualifies, so confirm through 311.
Timing tips
Schedule exterior paint for late spring to early fall, and other exterior work for when the weather warms up.
Interior vanilla-box work can happen year-round.
Start before the space is listed, so it shows well from day one.
The bottom line
In retail, presentation sells. A clean storefront, a code-ready vanilla box and a clear improvement offer can turn a long-vacant unit into a signed lease.
